Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
On 9 Nov 2001, Jeroen wrote:

> Legbiter's newsletter gave me an idea: If a number of us give a top 5
> (or 10) "Most Hated cards When Played By Someone Else", it might be
> possible to make a Most Hated Deck.

I don't have any static answer to this question, since the cards I hate,
and think about, and plan for, drift with the metagame. Actually, I think
it is the running response to this question which fuels the metagame. The
only reason I hate them at any given time is that they stymie a certain
deck to which I am partial and force me to consider other, perhaps more
well-trodden, paths to victory.

That said, off the top of my head:

1. The Embrace.

I personally dislike weenie decks. When performed successfully, Embracing
weenies add an order of magnitude to the problem.

2. Kindred Restructure/Dramatic Upheaval

In sufficient amounts, dissolves the game into noise. Predator-prey
relationships are viewed as the shifty, tenuous things they are. What's
the point of doing "x", since everything could be radically shifted at any
moment? Promotes existentialism, and moving the seating arrangement is a
pain in the ass.

3. Kiss of Ra

In a metagame heavy with fortitude and dominate, this card can more or
less dictate that yes, you too are playing with fortitude. Or never
block. Kiss of Ra/Freak/Graverobbing is sick.

4. Form of Mist

Here my arguments start getting even less objective. It just has
something to do with my belief that total minion actions are what
generally determine the winner of the game. This card amplifies minion
actions in a sense by halving the number of effective blockers the
opponent has available. The damn thing should at least cost something.

5. Rotschrek/White Phosphorous Grenade

I've been through the Rotschrek redefinitions, and I like the current one
best. I can live with the OOT rush/Rotschrek loophole. But using the
same grenade over and over again is stupid. This one certainly isn't
overpowered; it just seems plain wrong.

Note that these were in no particular order. I would've ordered them post
hoc except I'm on a crappy, encryption-lagged, terminal session.

David Cherryholmes
Prince of Durham

Skin of Steel? The frequency at which I see Carrion Crows has caused
me to modify my Fortitude defense packages.

My biggest gripe about Temptation of Greater Power and Hostile Takeover
is that the only real defense against their being played is a Sudden
Reversal. Their effect seems too great given the extremely limited
countermeasure options. Funny that you hate ToGP and Hostile Takeover
most, and then list Sudden Reversal at 5th place. ;) I think Parity
Shift looks a lot less strong when you take it outside of the context
of ToGP and Hostile Takeover (but it's still a strong card).

Direct Intervention, while occasionally handy, is soooooo overrated.
My biggest gripe about it is that it breaks the theme of Methuselahs
being purely puppeteers. Apart from that, master phase actions are
typically much stronger than an individual minion card, and as such,
trading the former to counter the latter is very typically too high
a price. You can almost always find a minion card countermeasure to
cover your butt. That being said, I'll put a DI or two in a weenie
deck to stop the occasional Anarchist Uprising/Ancilla Empowerment in
case my intercept can't cover it, or in a deck without superior Auspex
if I'm concerned about Perfect Clarity dorks.

I don't like Conditioning in casual play, but I think it's perfectly
fine otherwise...

Deflection, on the other hand, is the card I'd put right up top at
#1 in my list. Yeah, I use it a lot myself, but it irritates me
every time I do. It was my hatred of this card, and the ubiquitous
bucket brigades of bleed bouncing that it caused, that led me to
create Short Leash Bleed. It infuriated me that basic method for
ousting your prey had been reduced to a complete joke. I thank you
and love you, Change of Target. You are my light and salvation.

> It's their ability to pull off ALL of these, plus Kiss of Ra [number 11] and
> Day Op/Daring the Dawn [number 12], that makes the Ventrue such a disgusting
> clan. Sorry, Ben.

Must...avoid...the...bait...

;)

Well, like I said, we've done a solid job over here of innoculating
ourselves against the Ventrue. It's not like you can look at the
tournament winning decks in the US from the past couple of years and
say that they typically have a specific anti-Ventrue component. However,
they do tend to pack a lot of general-purpose things that are effective
against them. Look at the Ventrue-heavy decks that have won in the US
in the past couple of years, and you'll see that they drop a lot of the
Ventrue in favor of things that help defeat the typical countermeasures.
I'm inclined to agree with Dave Zopf's assessment that the Ventrue
provide a great supporting cast, rather than being great stand-alone.

But if you're playing an intercept deck, then leaving a minion
untapped shouldn't be that big of a deal. And you should have Forced
Awakenings and/or Animalism untaps which won't kill your hand size
like Wake will (and the untaps will get around Change of Target).

If you're not playing an intercept deck, then a single Lost in Crowds
will hose you just as much as a Change of Target, except that the
action will actually get through rather than needing to try again. So
how come you hate CoT more than Lost in Crowds?

The only thing that doesn't cover is bleed bounce. CoT will sort of
hose bleed bounce, which is nice. Bleed bounce is the cheasiest
cheese ever. The first tournament I went to, I played in a game that
had 4 decks with heavy bounce, and bleeds usually went all the way
around the table to stop at the guy without bounce. That's crap. Not
to mention that the best bleed bounce is in dominate, but I won't go
into that here.

On top of that, you're *supposed* to need an untapped minion in order
to block. If you want to block, you leave a guy untapped, otherwise
you just take what's handed to you. Wake kinda lets you cheat and get
around this restriction, but it's not without its weaknesses, in that
you're not actually untapped but are just pretending like you are. I

multiple extreme-weenie POT vampires, based largely around Hasina,

Multiple copies of each in crypt. Masters consisting largely of Info
Highway and Effective Management, with an Elder Library thrown in.

combo: Rush, IG, Undead Strength, Disarm, Amaranth.

need the Amaranth (with the weenie advantage, a second vampire such as
Uriah or Hasina can always be sent to diablerize after the beating), and

prey. This leaves you vulnerable to a lot more defenses, of course.

mutualling with your vampire in another way (Carrion Crows). But
against a combat-weak table, it could conceivably burn every single
vampire of its predator and prey that came out, and bleed for 1 lots if
no vamps arrived. Your opening crypt can cost you no more than 8...
probably less.

because the metagame is shifting towards combat and "hitting back
harder" than a punch for 2 isn't so uncommon anymore. But it
illustrates my objection to Disarm's inferior quite well; Hasina burning

I think that the "focused versus all-over-the-place" debate (I
supposed the "other side" might call it the "toolboxed versus narrowly
single-minded" debate) still has merit. I know that the debate has
been dragged on at length, but I think that a) it has not been drawn
to an obvious conclusion, like the CL vs. NCL argument, and b) it has
not been shown to be an unarguable point, like the argument over
Minion Tap (I could be wrong about this, maybe it *is* unarguable).

IMHO, a focused deck is nearly always better when you can accurately
predict the metagame, even as a general thing. If you can say, "the
metagame will have a lot of stealth," then you increase your chances
of winning by not throwing in minor intercept or too many wakes. If
you can say, "the metagame will have a lot of bleed bounce," then you
increase your chances of winning by not playing a heavy bleed deck.

It seems to me that a toolboxed deck only has an advantage over a
focused deck (all other things being equal) when the focused deck has
innacurately judged the metagame, since the toolboxed deck does not
even really try (or at least doesn't try *too* hard) to predict and
react. The toolboxed deck is ready for anything which is somewhat
likely to occur. In effect, it takes a value of METAGAME = 0, whereas
a focused deck tries to guess at a value.

If that dichotomy is correct, then it seems that if you expect a lot
of Change of Target in your metagame, you are better off playing a
focused deck that can deal with that, rather than an unfocused deck,
which is just the type of deck that Change of Target seems perfect
against. In a sealed deck type of environment, Change of Target
becomes a very good card. In a focused environment, such as I was
used to and very happy with playing under until about the release of
Final Nights, CoT is just not very useful.

Still not sure what my ultimate point is here... The above paragraphs
almost got snipped like the last few in my last post, but take them as
you will.

Winthrops, and 2 news locations. However, such a deck could not
reliably generate +2 intercept, in addition to reliably being able to
Wake. Unless you're playing an intercept deck, each Wake already
makes your deck less focused. Having, say, 6 Wakes seems like an
acceptable level of soft focus (smearing some butter on the lens, like
they do in porn movies), and maybe 4-5 intercept permanents, but I
can't see how such a deck could get 2 of those permanents out every
game. Once you *do* get those 2 permanents out (probably 10 turns
into the game), then how many Wakes do you have left? If you use 3
before you get them out (assuming you draw that many), and don't ever
get to the last wake in the deck, then you maybe get 2
intercept-worthy wakes.

That's not what I call "reliably" generating +2 intercept after you
wake. And the fact that the intercept is all permanent means that CoT
won't hurt you unless you are in the process of Waking. Lost in
Crowds, Earth Control, Shadow Play, etc., however, could hurt you
regardless.

Note that the numbers are completely speculation, but you'd be hard
pressed to get much better than that, unless you stack the deck to
always draw what you need. In my environment, any deck that isn't a
very focused combat deck will never draw out all the way, and
certainly will not draw more than half the deck in 10 turns. Is yours
different? Or do you just reliably draw all your intercept locations
on the first turn?

How is my prey tapped out? I bleed, he bounces. He spends 1 blood
and his prey loses 1 pool. I lose an action. His vampire is still
untapped. This is the *worst case scenario* of bleed bounce (worst
case to the bouncer), that he uses up 1 blood to bleed his prey for 1
(actually, I guess worst case is that I don't bleed, but other than
that). If bleed bounce were somehow useful when there are only 2
people left at the table, then the unbalance would run rampant and no
one would ever play anything but bounce, because even in the worst
case scenario, you spend one blood and one card to make your prey lose
a pool and your predator lose an action (or you spend one blood and
one card to make both your predator and prey both lose a blood, via
the default hands/hands combat). It's only the inability to bounce
when you're the last two decks on the table that really weakens bounce
at all. It's like the inverse of intercept, good for the first 3 vps,
bad for the last 2.

> You bleed, ask for blockers, no block, Conditioning (or whatever), bounce? -
> grand prey blocks, block - um, okay, that's what your minimal number of combat
> cards are for assuming your prey can fight at all.
>

Assuming your grandprey isn't tapped out. In most cases you just end
up hitting for one, but even this is strong. For one blood and a
Deflection, your prey basically cancels your bleed (like a free block
where he doesn't have to generate intercept and doesn't tap), and also
causes your vampire and one of your prey's vampires to each lose a
blood. That's strong already. On top of that, if you or your
grandprey screw up, then he may end up causing a huge amount of damage
to his prey.

It's probably silly to have this argument about bounce. I do agree
that bounce wouldn't be a bad thing if it were not given to dominate.
If it was given to auspex (and yes, Auspex has bounce, but it's not as
good as deflection), then you'd basically have a choice between
intercept or bounce with the same discipline (although bounce would
still usually be better). If it was given to chimerstry or
dementation, you'd have an interesting ability for an
out-of-the-ordinary discipline.

As it is, dominate is just a big red gaping design flaw. Huge bleeds
are somewhat unbalancing, except for the existence of bleed bounce.
Bleed bounce is somewhat unbalancing too, in that it hoses not only
big bleed, but can also be pretty useful against small bleeds. I just
think that we've lived with it long enough to become used to it. I
guess I feel the same way about bounce as a lot of people feel about
Minion Tap (which I don't feel is overpowered). And I can see the
flipside of the coin, that the fact that bounce is necessary to stop
big bleeds is just part of the game. If you expect big bleeds,
especially at stealth, then you gotta pack some bounce. If you're
gonna bleed, especially for large amounts or at stealth, then you
gotta be able to counter bleed bounce.

I'm not saying it's unbeatable, just unbalancing, and IMHO it always
has been.

An alternate viewpoint on toolbox decks is "METAGAME = some", in that
they expect the metagame to have a variety of deck styles, any of which
could crush them if they're not adequately prepared. Over the course
of the qualifying rounds of a tournament, you'll face 9-16 different
opponents. You can reasonably expect to face a decent variety of deck
types within those 9-16 decks.

Sure, if you guess the metagame correctly, you'll have an advantage
with a focussed deck. However, the toolbox fans prefer to not leave
their success up to chance.

Look at the decks of the finalists of the North American Championship.
(http://www.thelasombra.com/road/nac_decks.htm) The only truly focussed
deck was Robert Goudie's Torpor Machine, and he most definitely did
guess the metagame correctly. Three of the decks (Jared Strait's, Trey
Morita's, and Stephen Fazio's) are clearly toolbox decks. Mine lies
somewhere in between - hedging my bet, I guess.

Were Morita, Fazio, and Strait "begging to be screwed over" by using
toolbox decks? Hardly not. They were minimizing the chance that they
would get screwed over by unfavorable deck matchups. All three still
packed an offense that was more than sufficient. Jared Strait is an
interesting example, as he's been a major threat over the past four
years (at least) using toolbox decks.

> have to do it all of the time as I have a penchant for stealth bleed. It

Oh, sure...I certainly don't point at Change of Target as the only
option. Spying Mission works. Meld With the Land works. A little
bit of effort will dig up some other cards that work. Restraint
is another key factor. Short Leash Bleed isn't called that just
because of the Changes of Target - not bleeding for a gazillion is
a key part of it, too. Flushing out Wakes and Deflections is essential
to successful bleeding, and Change of Target is just one tool you can
use.

I've got a number of reasons for picking Change of Target...

I bleed...defender attempts to block...I play Bonding at superior...
defender Deflects...I tap the Rumor Mill to let my grandprey block...
I play Change of Target to untap both my guy and my grandprey's guy.
My grandprey doesn't spend any resources to defend, and my guy is now
untapped and ready to block/bounce, and I can send in a different guy
to bleed.

I bleed...defender Wakes and attempts to block...I play Change of Target
and leave the twerp tapped. My guy is untapped and ready to block or
bounce, and I can send in a different guy to bleed against a weakened
defender.

I bleed...predator (or whoever) unexpectedly plays Eagle's Sight and
I'm not prepared for his intercept...I play Change of Target and bail
out my vampire.

Instead of having to keep a couple guys back to block, and only use a
couple guys to bleed, I'm free to use all my minions in a given turn
for the bleed effort. If one or more get blocked, I can use Change of
Target and recover some minions for use as blockers/bouncers and send
the rest in to bleed. If the first couple are successful, I can stay
defensive with the other two or go for the jugular.

In general, I've found that Change of Target gives me much more freedom
to act.

strategy. I suppose it's possible for such a deck to win, perhaps
even win often. However, this is certainly "all-over-the-place"

I'm not sure it is more efficient. Consider that you can play your
own masters and still get "advanced" your next MPA to play a Sudden
on your prey's turn. Not to mention that there are ways to increase
your available MPAs. And then, the effectiveness of ToGP, Hostile,
and TGBall is just as dependent on what your opponents play as Sudden:
ToGP and Hostile are only good if your prey/predator are playing
non-weenies; TGBall if people were going to block your non-bleed
actions.

In master cards, I really don't believe that the best defense *is*
a good offense. Your offensive master cards in no way counter anyone
else's (unless you ToGP your opponent's only Justicar before he gets
a chance to do the same to yours - lucky at best). Sudden Reversal
is the only thing that actually *is* a defense against such masters.

Additionally, there are only a few strictly "offensive" master cards
available: ToGP, Hostile, Anarch Revolt, and such. Most of your
"good offense" masters are more like "strengthen my own position"
masters: skill cards, Blood Dolls, Minion Taps, etc. Against those,
Sudden acts more like an offensive card than a defensive one: you're
not going to play them against just *any* of your 3-4 opponents;
you're going to play them on your prey (when he tries to get out of
a tight spot) or your predator (when he tries to screw you).

Certainly not every deck wants to play Suddens, but from my point
of view, a dogmatic refusal to play Sudden is just as silly as
refusing to play Minion Taps would be: they're great cards that
can cause very large swings in the balance of power.

It is more efficient. If I use an MPA for me, I'm plus one good advantage for
myself in comparison to three other players. Other players need their own MPAs
to match that. If I use an MPA to cancel an opponent's MPA, I'm no better off
and he's no better off but our other two or three opponents can go advance
their own position with their own MPAs and neither of us can do a thing about
it. The fact that I'm "advanced" an MPA means exactly zero - I pay with my
ability to use an MPA later. (This seems pretty basic - perhaps I'm confused about
the point you're trying to make. But the fact that I can use my MPA in this turn
and Sudden Reverse before my next turn doesn't change anything in the long run as
near as I can tell.)

As for there being ways to increase my available MPAs, that also doesn't
enter into this argument. If I have two MPAs per turn, by the same reasoning
as above, it's still more efficient to grab *two* advantages for myself than
grab only one and cancel out one of my three or four opponent's advantages.
If I have three MPAs, better to grab three advantages than to grab only two
and cancel out an opponent's advantages.

> ToGP and Hostile are only good if your prey/predator are playing
> non-weenies; TGBall if people were going to block your non-bleed

a Sudden Reversal is "safer" in the sense that you can always hold it
to use against the plays that actually hurt you significantly vs. the
ones that don't. I guess I can only state that in my experience, my
MPAs are very seldom that ineffective. Like someone else in this thread
said, if I have a deck that actually has extra master slots, I'll begin
to consider Sudden Reverses (after a bunch of other generalized things
have been checked: The Barrens, Dreams of the Sphinx, Elder Library,
et al) but those are *very* rare. The vast majority of the time I deck
build, I'm gritting my teeth counting out master cards and eliminating
ones I'd love to have in the deck because I just can't use that many masters.
There ain't no room for a "safe" general master card in there.

> a good offense. Your offensive master cards in no way counter anyone
> else's (unless you ToGP your opponent's only Justicar before he gets
> a chance to do the same to yours - lucky at best).

No, but the "plus-one-for-me vs. minus-one-for-one-of-multiple-opponents"
logic is inevitable. Master card slots are far too important to be using
for the relatively limited benefit of stopping a single opponent from
using a single MPA.

> It is more efficient. If I use an MPA for me, I'm plus one good advantage for

> and Sudden Reverse before my next turn doesn't change anything in the long run as
> near as I can tell.)

I don't know about this +1 advantage logic. It seems to me far
too non-specific to be a useful analysis of VTES. For one thing,
there aren't many masters that are *always* advantageous when you
draw them. Hunting Grounds are useless if (a) you don't have the
right clan of vampire or (b) don't have any vampires that need
blood; Blood Doll is useless if your vampires don't have any blood
to give you and you can't afford to give it to them; Minion Tap
is useless if you don't have any Tappable vampires; KRCG is useless
if you don't need intercept; Barrens is useless if you don't need
an extra discard... everything is situationally contingent.

Yes, you expect the "advantage" masters you put in your deck to
be useful to you, but likewise you expect your prey's "advantage"
masters to be worth cancelling. As such, it seems to me that
playing with Sudden Reversals is worth doing when your deck is
happier using your master phase actions to mess up your prey than
to improve your own position.

After all, it really doesn't matter if you're falling behind in
the "advantage arms race" against your grandpredator, grandprey,
or possibly even predator. You win the game by ousting your prey,
not by building up "advantages". If Suddens make it easier to
oust your prey, they may be the most useful master available.

(the "master phase on credit" point I was trying to make was:
you can, at least in theory, destabilize the table in your favor
by playing an "advantage" master of your own and then, in the
same time around the table, preventing your prey from getting
an "advantage" master. That puts you at +1 vs your prey, compared
to if both of you successfully played "advantages", which is good
in your book, right? Yes, next time around, you don't get to play
an "advantage" and your prey does, but just like with money, it's
better to get your advantage earlier than later.)

> As for there being ways to increase my available MPAs, that also doesn't
> enter into this argument. If I have two MPAs per turn, by the same reasoning
> as above, it's still more efficient to grab *two* advantages for myself than
> grab only one and cancel out one of my three or four opponent's advantages.
> If I have three MPAs, better to grab three advantages than to grab only two
> and cancel out an opponent's advantages.

I really don't agree with that; if you could get the draw to do it,
it would usually be *much* better to play one advantage per turn
and keep your prey from getting *any* than to play two advantages
per turn.

> That's true but I consider it to be kind of irrelevant. I do see how
> a Sudden Reversal is "safer" in the sense that you can always hold it
> to use against the plays that actually hurt you significantly vs. the
> ones that don't. I guess I can only state that in my experience, my
> MPAs are very seldom that ineffective. Like someone else in this thread

> There ain't no room for a "safe" general master card in there.

You might want to try building a deck around playing lots of Suddens
sometime and see how it works for you (maybe you've already done
this and found that it was no good, I don't know). If your prey is
playing defensive masters, Suddens are actually more offensive than
your own offensive masters. :-)

> No, but the "plus-one-for-me vs. minus-one-for-one-of-multiple-opponents"
> logic is inevitable. Master card slots are far too important to be using
> for the relatively limited benefit of stopping a single opponent from
> using a single MPA.

> It's not dogmatic. It's based on very sound logic which seems to

The thing is, there are certain decks that lend themselves to powerful
master cards. MTs with big vamps, ToGP, Hostile Takeover. There are
also decks that really rely on master cards in order to work well.
Out-of-clan disciplines, Anarch Revolts, those crazy Madness Network
themed decks. And finally, there are really good master cards that
can sometimes turn the tide of a game. Zillah's Valley, Smiling Jack,
KRCG, stealth locations.

If you are in a position to use these cards, then throw them in. Skip
the SRs. But some decks are not in a position to use the really
strong masters, or at least not to be able to gain full effect out of
them. If I could play a Dreams of the Sphinx but don't really need
it, I might get 50% use out of it, so I get a .5 master advantage by
playing it. If I SR *your* Dreams of the Sphinx (or ZV, or MT...
note that if I was *only* worried about DotS, I could just use it to
contest), which you were going to use to 100% effect, I keep you from
getting a 1.0 master advantage. If you are my prey, I'd prefer to
gain a 1.0 master advantage on you than to gain a .5 master advantage
on the table. (actually, it's the difference between staying *even*
and allowing *you* to gain a .5 master advantage on me).

When I make a deck, I generally put in the masters that the deck
*needs* first. Next are the slots for masters that might help, and SR
is included in these. Very often, my combat decks, if they have
enough discipline cards, will have 2 SRs in them, which are quite
often put to good use. If I have the choice of playing something like
an Elder Library, which could make my life a little easier and might
help me out, or stop my opponent from playing that Protean master that
he's really relying on, I'll go for the SR. There's definitely a
frustration that you get from having your masters cancelled, and it's
even better if you were planning your whole turn around that master.

And SRing an Ascendance is just funny. 8)

Perhaps. Yes, it's another library denial card. Yes, it's potentially
annoying.

It will, in general, hurt a toolboxed deck - with a number of prayer
cards - more than a focused deck, where any card that goes is likely to
feature in the deck multiple times.

It's not unbeatable, it's not stupidly over-powered and it is limited to
a unique resource - a vampire - which does make it hard to abuse, for a
multiplicity of reasons, many of which are obvious.

It also has the problem of lumping you with a card you can't use until
you can get rid of it. And if you don't use the special because chances
are they'll have *nothing* you can use, well, that's part of the costing
wasted.

>If I have a thaum strike coming up for my thaum skilled
>vampires, why should this vampire be able to swipe it from me and even
>possibly use it against me?

In simple terms, Just Because (tm).

The whole paradigm of the Methuselah controlling exactly what strike is
employed (taking a Strike: card as an example) is slightly screwed up
anyway, from a back-story point of view. Even in the Jyhad, a vampire
will be able to choose if it hits with Discipline X or defends with
Discipline Y.

However, if we establish that a vampire can undermine a Methuselah's
resources - by making them discard their library, as was established in
the very first printing with Dr. Jest, as an example - then it is not a
huge leap from being able to undermine those resources to being able to
steal some of those resources, in a limited manner.

The specifics of the situation will often not quite stand up to
"logical" back-story based scrutiny.
